newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul stocks end lower 1996 last trading day.
newsitem.headline: Seoul stocks end lower 1996 last trading day.

text.p: Stocks closed sharply lower on Friday, the last trading day of 1996 as spreading labour unrest dampened already weak investor sentiment, brokers said.
The composite index provisionally ended at 651.22, the lowest closing level this year. This was down 7.79 points or 1.18 percent on the day.
The index was down 26.24 percent from 882.94 at the end of 1995.
Declining stocks overwhelmed advancers by 729 to 218.
Brokers said deteriorating labour situation, sparked by Thursday's passage of a new labour law, remained the biggest single factor dampening the market.
Strikes spread wider as nurses and orderlies closed out-patient sections of 14 hospitals, joining workers at major carmakers and shipyards.
Union wrath is aimed at the fact that the new labour law gives employers the right to lay off surplus workers, introduce flexible working hours and replace strikers.
"The brief rebound towards the close of the morning failed to gain further momentum because of worries over the labour strife," said Ha Yong-hyun of Hyundai Securities.
Brokers earlier said some blue chips rebounded from early sharp falls as public pension funds started buying these shares to support the index. This was not independently confirmed.

Samsung Electronics closed 800 won higher at 45,500, after falling to its daily limit of 43,500 in the morning. But Korea Electric Power ended the day 400 won lower at 24,600 after rising to an intraday high of 25,200.
Half an hour after the closing bell, Finance Minister Han Seung-soo announced the government would draft a new bill to raise living standards and improve employment conditions.
He said the bill would include steps to improve vocational training for workers, offer skilled workers greater opportunities and stabilise salaries and living standards.
But brokers said the announcement, which gave no further details on the proposed new bill, was unlikely to effectively soothe labour outrage.
The market will be closed for trading until January 2.
